speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was the shortest length of time that you were working in Princeton?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Spokane. We moved there in September, in April.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your husband was away from you all the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, he was working down in Princeton.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you think about the separation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't like it. We were going to get a job in Spokane, but woods were paid much better. So that's why we went.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I always wondered, my father was in the service, and my mother died when I was a junior at the university. I always would like to ask her how she felt during a year of separation, when he was over here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I imagine it was pretty hard on her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do to take up the time that you would have been spending with your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I cut the house clean, and a neighbor, a couple houses from me, I had gone with her boy during the war, he went to the University of Idaho, with the NAVES, what is it they call it, with the army there. I went down to Moscow to visit, and when I went to Spokane, this lady came to see me, and found out that I mentioned my name. She said, I remember that name, my name, didn't you go with a boy by the name of Harold Luke? I said, yeah, he's always talking about you. So I had a friend, and we visited all the time. I'd go downtown with her in the daytime, before I started work. But we moved there just as Joy started school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where did you go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She worked in the hospital, that's how I got a job right away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But she was older than I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did Joy go to school after Moscow, Spokane?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At Avon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did she go there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Until she was in the sixth grade, we moved up here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you think education has changed since you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Very, very much. I wouldn't even know how to go to school now. I wouldn't know what to do. So many, you have a teacher for each subject, and in those days, a teacher taught everything. And we had nothing but book work and pencil and paper. Where now you have your lab work. And really experiment with things. Cooking.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think you would like to go to school as it is now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just as we have now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which do you think you would like better?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of which?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Of the way that you were taught versus the way that people are taught now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's much better now. You have a more liberal education.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember when the school started being consolidated? How did you feel about that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, living in Kellogg, I didn't think much about it. But we were, my husband was going to work up at Fernwood, and my daughter would have had to ridden a bus from Fernwood to St. Mary's, the school. Which was in ninth grade, and I didn't think... What do you do with this stuff when you get it collected?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, this will go to the archives at the University of Idaho. And then if people are doing research, then they can use it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Can you save days for this? You mean I pay for this?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I thought so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I thought so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does he not like government projects?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He doesn't like government projects at all. His day pays taxes and taxes. Well, he'll soon be, so one-fourth of the people take care of three-fourths of the people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that the way that you feel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the way he feels. How do you feel about it? Well, I don't know. People have to be taken care of. In the olden days, you had someone in your locality that was fired up. All the neighbors would give this and that to help them along. But if the man was able to work and didn't work, they soon got him to working. And they made him work. It was worth it. Now you can't do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any modern... anything about modern life that you don't like now? Or modern conveniences?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Nothing on modern conveniences that I do not like. But I... I'm not giving you much information.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, what else is there about... or is there anything about modern society that you don't like?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think the parents should have a little closer watch on their children when they're out at play. Instead of saying, go out, out to play, but don't bother me. And fight your own battles. Don't tattle on the other children. I think parents should be told sometimes, that these things have happened. And then they should tell their child that they should do these things. And then rather see that they don't do them. Instead of, oh, the other child is at fault. Find out the deep down thing. I rent houses. I have children in my yard all the time, and other children. And I myself would be out there if they were playing with these other children. Because the environment isn't right. You can't trust your children with, oh lord. Explaining a few things to them. That there's certain things they should tell their parents about the children. But other things, when it's just a fight or something, you can understand the things that go on that the little child knows is right, and should tell his parents. So the parents should talk to these children sometimes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you prefer your way of life now, as opposed to when you were growing up? Do you just kind of accept it as it is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's just the time to go along with them. If things had been as they are now, when I grew up, but I was young, I don't think my parents would have done it. I wouldn't have played with any of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I know that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But they were very strict. My daughter says, well, Mother, you were pretty strict in one way. You watched, you see that I had the right kind of friends. I never was allowed to go to a person's home. If you let your parents, your children, then she could go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that's the thing.
